title: Weddings in Crete: Venues, Paperwork and Costs

body:
Crete is one of the most popular islands in Greece for a destination wedding, and it is not hard to see why. It has Venetian harbour towns, mountain villages, long stretches of coast, real food, and enough infrastructure to move a hundred guests around without improvising. It is also large — considerably larger than most couples expect — which is the single thing that catches wedding parties out.

This guide covers the practical side: where couples actually marry, what the civil ceremony paperwork involves, what it costs, when to do it, and how to get your guests from the airport to the ceremony and back.

## Why couples choose Crete

Crete works as a wedding destination for a few concrete reasons. It has two international airports, Heraklion and Chania, with direct flights from most of Europe through the summer — so guests can usually get there in one hop. It has a long season, roughly April to late October. And it offers genuinely different settings within a few hours' drive: a Venetian harbour, an olive grove, a mountain village, a beach on the Libyan Sea.

It also has an established wedding industry. Municipalities in the main towns handle civil ceremonies for foreign couples routinely, and there is a deep bench of local planners, photographers, caterers and venues who do this every week in season.

## Where to get married in Crete

The island splits into four regions, and which one you pick shapes everything else — including how far your guests have to travel.

| Region | Airport logic | Suits | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chania and the west | Chania airport close; Heraklion is roughly three hours away | Couples who want Venetian old-town character and the island's most photographed beaches | Guests who book the wrong airport face a long transfer |
| Rethymno and the centre | About an hour from Chania airport, about an hour and a half from Heraklion | Guest lists split across flights into both airports | Fewer large single-site resort venues than the east |
| Heraklion, Elounda and the east | Heraklion airport | Five-star resort weddings with everything on one site; close to Knossos | Furthest from the western scenery most guests picture |
| The south coast | Either, via slower mountain roads | Small weddings and elopements where the setting matters most | Slower roads and scattered accommodation make large groups hard |

### Chania and the west

Chania's Venetian harbour is the postcard image of Crete, and the old town is one of the prettiest in Greece. The west also has the island's most photographed beaches — Elafonisi and Balos. It is a strong choice if the look of the place matters most. The trade-off is that the far west is a long way from Heraklion airport, so guests flying into the wrong airport face a three-hour transfer.

### Rethymno and the centre

Rethymno sits between the two airports, roughly an hour from Chania airport and an hour and a half from Heraklion. That makes it the most forgiving base when guests are arriving on flights into both. It has its own Venetian old town, a long town beach, and quick access to traditional villages, gorges and the south coast. For a wedding party split across multiple flights, the logistics are simply easier here.

### Heraklion, Elounda and the east

The east is where the large luxury resorts are, particularly around Elounda and Agios Nikolaos. If you want a five-star resort wedding with everything on one site, this is the end of the island to look at. It is also close to Knossos and the main archaeological sites.

### The south coast

Quieter, more rugged, and less developed — Plakias, Preveli, Matala, Loutro. Good for small weddings and elopements where the setting matters more than the guest count. Harder for large groups: the roads are slower and the accommodation is more scattered.

## The legal side: what a civil wedding in Crete involves

A civil wedding, performed by a mayor, deputy mayor or authorised civil official, is the route most foreign couples take. It is a real legal marriage and is normally recognised internationally. The paperwork is where the time goes.

### What you will be asked for

In broad terms, couples are typically asked for:

- Valid passports — originals plus photocopies
- Birth certificates for both parties
- A Certificate of No Impediment (CNI) for each party, confirming you are legally free to marry, obtained from your own country's authorities or embassy
- Divorce decrees or death certificates, if either party has been married before
- An application form submitted to the municipality where you are marrying

Documents from outside Greece generally need to be legalised — usually with an Apostille stamp — and officially translated into Greek by a recognised translator. The ceremony itself is conducted in Greek or English, with an interpreter if needed and two witnesses present.

### Two timings that catch people out

Most guidance suggests starting the legal process six to twelve months before the wedding, because obtaining and legalising a CNI can take weeks. And after the ceremony, the marriage must be registered with the Civil Registry — commonly cited as within 40 days — for full legal recognition.

Municipal fees for a civil ceremony are commonly quoted in the range of roughly €100 to €550, depending on the municipality and on whether the ceremony is at the town hall or at an approved outside venue.

Please confirm all of this directly. Requirements differ between municipalities and change over time, and they depend on your own nationality. Contact the municipality where you intend to marry and your own country's embassy or consulate in Greece early in the process, and — if you are not living in Greece — consider working with a local wedding planner who handles the submissions routinely. Nothing here is legal advice.

## What a wedding in Crete costs

Costs vary enormously, and anyone quoting you a single figure is guessing. The honest answer is that the range is driven by four things: guest count, venue type, season, and how much of the work you hand to a planner.

| Cost line | What it covers | What moves the number | Published figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Municipal ceremony fee | The civil ceremony itself | Which municipality; town hall or approved outside venue | Roughly €100–€550 |
| Document handling | Translation, Apostille legalisation, couriers | Your nationality and how many documents need legalising | Quote-driven |
| Venue | The site and, often, a minimum spend | Town-hall-and-taverna at one end; private villa or resort takeover at the other | Quote-driven |
| Catering and drinks | The meal and bar | Priced per head — usually the largest single line for a mid-sized wedding | Quote-driven |
| Planner | Coordination and supplier management | Either a percentage of total spend or a flat fee | Quote-driven |
| Photography, flowers, music, hair and make-up | The day itself | Scope and season | Quote-driven |
| Guest transport | Airport arrivals, hotel-to-venue, the return, departures | Guest count, how many hotels, how spread the flights are | Quote-driven — and routinely underestimated |

A small ceremony with a dozen guests and a restaurant dinner is a fundamentally different budget from an eighty-guest villa wedding in August. Get quotes for your actual guest count and date rather than working from a published average.

## When to get married in Crete

The season runs roughly from April to late October. May, early June, September and early October are the sweet spot: warm, settled, long evenings, and noticeably less crowded than midsummer. Most planners will push you here.

Late July and August are the hottest and busiest months. Temperatures inland regularly make an afternoon outdoor ceremony uncomfortable, flights and accommodation are at peak prices, and venues book out earliest. It can be done well — it just needs the timings built around the heat, with the ceremony late in the day.

April and late October are cheaper and quieter, with a real chance of rain and cooler evenings. Fine if you have a covered fallback, risky if you do not.

## Getting your guests around the island

This is the part that most often goes wrong, and it is worth planning early.

The problem is scale. Crete is about 260 km end to end, and driving times are longer than the distances suggest because much of the road network is coastal or mountainous. Guests will arrive at two different airports, on flights spread across two or three days, and they will not all be staying in the same hotel. Public transport between regions is limited and does not run to flight schedules.

In practice a wedding group needs transport for four distinct movements:

1. **Arrivals** — airport to accommodation, spread across many separate flights
2. **The wedding day** — multiple hotels to one venue, timed to the ceremony
3. **The return** — venue back to accommodation, late, after a long evening
4. **Departures** — accommodation to airport, again spread out

Leaving guests to arrange their own taxis works for a party of ten and falls apart somewhere around thirty. Beyond that, coordinated group transport is both cheaper per head and far more likely to get everyone to the ceremony on time.

Way to Crete handles exactly this. We are based in Rethymno and run wedding transfers and guest transportation — airport transfers from Heraklion and Chania, hotel-to-venue transport on the day, the return afterwards, and private excursions for guests staying on either side of the wedding. Note that we operate within the Rethymno region, including transfers to and from both airports; we do not currently run transfers within the Chania, Heraklion or Lassithi regions.

### Give your guests something to do

Most wedding guests stay for the best part of a week, and a destination wedding is an easier sell if there is more to it than one evening. A group excursion in the days around the wedding — a food and wine day, a village and monastery tour, a cooking class — does more for the weekend than another afternoon by the pool, and gets people talking to each other before the wedding day itself.

## A realistic planning timeline

| When | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 12+ months out | Pick the region and the date. Enquire at venues, especially for June to September. |
| 9–12 months | Book the venue. Appoint a planner if you are using one. Start the legal paperwork: check requirements with the municipality and your embassy. |
| 6–9 months | Send save-the-dates so guests can book flights while they are cheap. Book photographer and catering. Begin obtaining and legalising documents. |
| 3–6 months | Collect guest arrival details: which airport, which flight, which hotel. This is when transport planning becomes possible. |
| 1–3 months | Confirm final numbers, finalise the transport schedule and pickup points, confirm timings with every supplier. |
| Final weeks | Submit the marriage licence application in person as required, and circulate the transport schedule to guests. |

## Planning a wedding in Crete?

If you are organising a wedding here — as a couple or as a planner — and you need the transport side handled, tell us your date, venue, guest numbers and where people are staying. We will come back with a plan.

faqs.q: Is a civil wedding in Crete legally recognised abroad?
faqs.a: A civil wedding performed by a mayor or authorised civil official in Greece is a legal marriage, and is generally recognised in other countries once the marriage certificate has been issued and, where required, apostilled and translated. Confirm the specific requirements with the authorities in your own country before you travel.

faqs.q: How far in advance should we start planning a wedding in Crete?
faqs.a: Most planners suggest starting 12 months out for a peak-season date, and beginning the legal paperwork six to twelve months before the ceremony. Popular venues in Chania and Rethymno book up well over a year ahead for June to September.

faqs.q: What is the best month to get married in Crete?
faqs.a: May, early June, September and early October are the usual recommendations — warm and settled but without the peak heat and crowds of late July and August. April and late October are cheaper and quieter, with a higher chance of unsettled weather.

faqs.q: Do we need to be in Crete before the wedding day?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Municipalities normally require the couple to submit documents in person and there is typically a short waiting period before the licence is issued, so most couples arrive several days ahead. Your municipality will confirm the exact requirement.

faqs.q: Which part of Crete is best for a destination wedding?
faqs.a: Chania and the west suit couples wanting Venetian old-town character and dramatic beaches. Rethymno sits in the middle of the island and is the easiest base if guests are flying into both airports. Elounda and the east are the luxury-resort end. The south coast is the quietest and most rugged.

faqs.q: How do wedding guests get around Crete?
faqs.a: Most guests fly into Heraklion or Chania and need transport to their accommodation, then to the venue and back on the day. Crete is large and public transport between regions is limited, so wedding groups usually arrange private or group transfers rather than leaving guests to organise individual taxis.

faqs.q: How much does a wedding in Crete cost?
faqs.a: There is no single figure. The only published number is the municipal ceremony fee, commonly quoted at roughly €100 to €550 depending on the municipality and whether you marry at the town hall or an approved outside venue. Everything else — venue, catering, planner, photography, transport — is quoted against your actual guest count, date and venue type.
